children.text: The Philippines' signature resort town, where black limestone islands rise out of Bacuit Bay and meet jade-green lagoons. Tours A through D take you island hopping through the Big Lagoon, secret beaches, and caves, and there's plenty more to enjoy too, from beach sunsets to kayaking and cliff climbing.

El Nido is a coastal town at the northern tip of Palawan Island, cradling Bacuit Bay. Inside the bay are dozens of islands formed when limestone laid down under the sea some 250 million years ago pushed up above the surface, each with sheer cliffs, hidden lagoons, and small strips of white sand. The name "El Nido" is Spanish for "nest," from the swiftlet nests — the ingredient for bird's nest soup — once harvested from crevices in the limestone cliffs.

The area is designated the El Nido–Taytay Managed Resource Protected Area, protecting coral reefs, mangroves, sea turtles, and dugong habitat. Tourism generally takes two forms. Most travelers stay in town and join the city-set Tours A, B, C, and D for island hopping, while some stay at private-island resorts such as Miniloc, Lagen, Pangulasian, and Apulit to enjoy a quieter sea.

El Nido's charm lies in the density of its scenery. The moment you kayak through a narrow channel between the cliffs and enter the Big Lagoon, the contrast between the jade water and black cliffs is overwhelming. At sunset, you can watch the sky turn red behind the silhouettes of islands from Las Cabanas Beach and Corong-Corong Beach, and from Taraw Cliff behind town, the whole bay unfolds below.

The town has grown quickly, and its narrow lanes are now packed tight with lodging, restaurants, and travel agencies; in peak season, tour boats crowd the most popular lagoons. So planning your itinerary and choosing your time slots carefully matters in El Nido. It's one of the first places to recommend to travelers who want both island hopping and beach relaxation, honeymooners, and anyone planning their first Philippine beach trip.
Administratively, it began in
as a municipality named Bacuit, and in
it took its present name, El Nido, under Republic Act No. 1140. As of the
census, it has about 51,000 residents and covers about 923 km². Bacuit Bay is dotted with 45 islands and islets, and the peak of the highest, Cadlao Island, stands about
above sea level. The El Nido–Taytay Managed Resource Protected Area was designated in

and is described as one of the Philippines' largest marine protected areas, made up of 40% land and 60% sea. Visitor numbers have grown fast: by lodging check-in registrations, about 640,000 people visited El Nido in
, the most in Palawan after Puerto Princesa.
El Nido's most famous route — kayak through a channel between the cliffs into the Big Lagoon. It's often combined with Secret Lagoon, Shimizu Island, and Seven Commandos Beach.

blocks.title: Tour C: hidden beaches and a shrine

children.text: A route through Hidden Beach and Secret Beach, reached only through a gap in the rocks, the abandoned shrine to the Virgin Mary on Matinloc Island, and the beach at Helicopter Island. Snorkeling spots are good here, and many say the scenery is the most dramatic of all.

blocks.title: Tour D: Small Lagoon and Cadlao

children.text: A relatively quiet route around Small Lagoon, Cadlao Lagoon, and Paradise Beach. A good choice if you want to see lagoons that don't overlap with Tour A.

blocks.title: Tour B: caves and a sandbar

children.text: A route to Snake Island, where an S-shaped sandbar appears at low tide, plus Cudugnon Cave and Cathedral Cave. The view of the sandbar from the Snake Island viewpoint is striking.

items.title: Compact 2-night, 3-day itinerary
items.subtitle: For a short stay covering just the two main tours

children.text: After arriving in town, drop your bags at your accommodation, pay the environmental fee (ETDF), and book two days of tours at a city-licensed travel agency
Sunset at Corong-Corong Beach or Las Cabanas Beach
Day 2: Tour A. Departure from the town pier is usually 08:30–09:00, and the route covers Big Lagoon, Secret Lagoon, Shimizu Island, and Seven Commandos Beach
Day 2: Seafood dinner at a restaurant in town, and confirm the departure time for the next day's tour
Day 3: Tour C (on a calm-sea day) or Tour B. Matinloc Shrine, Hidden Beach, and snorkeling at Helicopter Island
Day 3: Return to town and confirm your airport transfer (vans to Puerto Princesa Airport include early-morning departures, so book the day before)

Tours cover one route per day. Big Lagoon and Small Lagoon are said not to be enterable on the same day, so to see both lagoons, plan the routes over two days and confirm at booking whether each is included.

There are direct flights to El Nido Airport (ENI, Lio Airport) from Clark, Cebu, Boracay (Caticlan), Bohol, and Coron (Busuanga). AirSwift, which used small propeller aircraft, was acquired by the Cebu Pacific group, and from
July 2026
its subsidiary Cebgo operates the same routes. From Clark it takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–1 hour 40 minutes
, with one-way fares on the expensive side at about
and strict baggage weight limits. The airport is about
4km
north of town, taking about
15–20 minutes
by resort shuttle or tricycle.
Since
March 29, 2026

, propeller aircraft have been banned from operating at Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport, so there are no longer direct Manila–El Nido flights. If you're departing from Manila, choose between taking a Genesis P2P bus from NAIA Terminal 3 to Clark Airport — about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
(about

There are also routes that bypass Manila. Cebgo flies direct between El Nido and Cebu (about
1 hour 45 minutes

1 hour 10 minutes

40 minutes

You can walk around town, and reach Las Cabanas, Corong-Corong, and Nacpan by tricycle (about

December
through
May
is the dry season and the best time to visit.
March–May
especially has the calmest sea and clearest water, ideal for lagoons and snorkeling, but during Holy Week and summer break, lodging prices rise and tour boats crowd in.
December–February
can be a bit windy with some choppy days, but the cooler temperatures make it good for walking.
From
June
to
October

, the southwest monsoon Habagat brings frequent rain, and on rough-sea days the coast guard halts tour departures or changes the route. Still, there are more days with passing showers than all-day rain, and lodging prices drop significantly, appealing to budget travelers. This period calls for building buffer days into your schedule. Northern Palawan sees fewer direct typhoon hits than central Philippines, but in some years a typhoon still passes through in
October–December
, so check the forecast.
Annual temperatures generally stay within
, and rain peaks around
August
. By lodging registrations, visitors were most concentrated in
January–May
and
November–December
in
, so book your lodging and early-morning tours first for these periods. Typhoons are no exception in northern Palawan. On
November 5, 2025

, Typhoon Tino (Kalmaegi) made landfall at El Nido, damaging homes, schools, and hospitals, and the Coast Guard blocked island-hopping departures. Don't relax just because November is the tail end of the rainy season; for trips in this period, check the forecast and your airline's change policy.

For a first visit, El Nido town (the Poblacion), close to the tour departure point, is convenient. A guesthouse runs about
per night, a mid-range hotel about

. For a quieter atmosphere, Corong-Corong Beach south of town and the Kalibang area are good, with many resorts offering great sunset views. The Las Cabanas side has a cluster of beach resorts, good for focusing on relaxation. The Lio Beach area to the north is a planned resort estate close to the airport, suited to families wanting clean facilities. The private-island resorts of Miniloc, Lagen, Pangulasian, and Apulit run tens of thousands of pesos a night, but include private lagoon tours and meals.

The food centers on fresh seafood. Island-hopping lunches are laid out by the boatmen — grilled fish, shrimp, pork barbecue, and mangoes and pineapple. Town restaurants range from Filipino food to Italian, Mexican, and vegetarian options, and in the evening it's popular to pick seafood displayed on ice at a beach restaurant, ordered by weight. Some places also sell tamilok, a Palawan specialty eaten raw — a shipworm that lives inside mangrove wood. Prices in town run higher than the Philippine average, so budget around
per meal.
By type of lodging, dorms run about

from town, so on an itinerary heavy on island hopping it's better to fit in just a day or two there. For meals, local eateries (carinderias) are cheapest at about

Town has several ATMs, but in peak season cash often runs out and fees are high. It's best to bring plenty of cash from Puerto Princesa or Manila.
Keep your environmental-fee receipt with you throughout your stay, since it's checked before every tour.
The popular lagoons are busiest at
. Chartering a private boat and leaving early in the morning, or reversing the tour order, makes it much quieter.
Entry to the Big Lagoon is sometimes managed by headcount and time slot, so confirm when booking your tour that lagoon entry is guaranteed.
A dry bag, aqua shoes, and a rash guard are essential — tours involve a lot of walking over rocks and coral.
Direct flights have strict cabin and checked baggage weight limits, so it's best to pack light.
Smart and Globe signals are good in town but drop out frequently between islands.
Las Cabanas Beach is the spot for sunset photos, and Taraw Cliff's summit and the Snake Island viewpoint are the spots for bay views.

Many places accept only cash for island-hopping tour fees, the environmental fee, lagoon entrance fees, and ziplines, so bring plenty of small ₱100 and ₱200 bills. Town ATMs have a per-withdrawal limit of about
and a fee of about
, so it pays to withdraw cash in advance in Manila or Puerto Princesa.
Island hopping usually departs from the town pier at
and returns at
4–5 PM
. A packed lunch, drinking water, snorkel gear, and a life vest are included as standard, and there is a rule that you can't enter both Big Lagoon and Small Lagoon on the same day.

To protect the coral and lagoons, coral collection, touching marine life, and bringing single-use plastics are banned, and rules change often by city tourism office notice, so check the latest updates.
Wear a life vest during island hopping, and avoid operators that push ahead on high-wave days.
The midday sun is very strong, causing frequent sunburn and dehydration. Bring reef-safe sunscreen and plenty of water.
Jellyfish appear at certain times of year, so wear a rash guard, and rinse with vinegar if stung.
Power and water in town sometimes cut out during peak season, so a power bank and a relaxed schedule help.
Unlicensed touts' tours may skip entrance fees and environmental fees or change the route, so it's safer to use city-licensed operators.
According to a
February 2025

report, fecal coliform in El Nido's coastal waters consistently exceeded the recommended swimming standard, and only about 3% of households in the town center were connected to sewers. It's better to swim at island-hopping spots than at the beach in front of town, and if you have an open wound, avoid entering the water at town beaches.
